title: Adult social care reform in England
key_claim: On 29 July 2026 the Prime Minister moved the Casey Commission's report to summer 2027 and dropped the two-phase plan; on 29 September 2026 he described a National Care Service free at the point of use. The Health Foundation's July 2026 estimates of extra annual cost by 2035/36 are about £4bn for a cap, £7.5bn for free personal and nursing care and £18.5bn for a universal system.
frame_summary: Sets out the reform timetable and the Health Foundation's three costed options as the factual base for the National Care Service debate.

title: Social care postcode lottery reveals variations in access to long-term care
key_claim: 59% of local authorities had publicly funded long-term care access rates at least 20% above or below those of their nearest statistical neighbours, with up to twice as many people supported per 100,000; Thurrock supported 7,680 older people per 100,000 against 4,810 in Medway.
frame_summary: Argues that access to publicly funded care is set by postcode, and that an equal-access national assessment and national funding would remove unwarranted variation.

title: Social care funding options for reform
key_claim: The Health Foundation estimates a universal and comprehensive system could cost about £18.5bn extra in 2035/36, and says the estimate does not include likely additional costs of people with unmet care needs.
frame_summary: Argues that the cost of each reform option depends on its design, and that the universal option is costed on current service users and so leaves out people with unmet need.

title: King's Fund calls for national funding model to underpin social care reforms
key_claim: The King's Fund wants national rather than local funding of social care and a cap on lifetime payments; one in seven people aged 65 will spend at least £100,000 in lifetime care costs.
frame_summary: Reports the King's Fund's case for a national funding model, a lifetime cap and an equal-access assessment as the basis of social care reform.

title: Burnham signals a stinging tax hike of billions to fund free social care
key_claim: The Prime Minister said reforms would be funded through a system in which everyone contributes, disputed an £18bn-a-year cost for a universal free-care system when asked on the BBC, and said manifesto commitments make it hard to deliver the reforms in this parliament.
frame_summary: Reads the Prime Minister's BBC interview as a signal that taxpayers will pay more for free social care while the cost and timing remain unsettled.

title: Adult social care under increasing pressure as new national survey highlights rising demand
key_claim: Reporting the ADASS Spring Survey, more than 400,000 people across England are waiting for an assessment, care and support; councils overspent adult social care budgets by £715 million in 2025/26; the number waiting for a carers assessment has risen significantly.
frame_summary: Reports the ADASS Spring Survey as evidence that rising demand is leaving councils over budget and people waiting for care.

title: Variation in access to adult social care: LGA response to the King's Fund report
key_claim: The LGA says variation in access stems from many factors including levels of affluence or deprivation in the local population, and calls for long-term, sustainable reform built on prevention.
frame_summary: Argues that differences in access between councils have local causes and that reform should be long-term and prevention-led with defined national and local roles.
